summary: This bill funds most federal agencies and programs for all of fiscal year 2025 by continuing 2024 spending levels with targeted adjustments and extends expiring health, Medicare, and other authorities through September 30, 2025.

scores.thoughts: The bill is a full-year continuing resolution that appropriates funds for FY2025 across all major government functions at or near FY2024 levels, with targeted adjustments, increases in some accounts, and rescissions in others (particularly defense). It directly authorizes and sustains discretionary spending rather than enacting broad reductions or new expansions, resulting in a modest negative score.
The legislation contains no provisions altering tax rates, credits, deductions, or revenue measures of any kind.

Division B extends community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, teaching health centers, special diabetes programs, Medicare payment adjustments, telehealth flexibilities, and delays Medicaid DSH reductions. These actions maintain and extend public-program funding and access provisions.
No provisions address firearms regulation, background checks, or gun rights.
DHS funding levels are continued with minor adjustments; no new policy changes expand or restrict immigration pathways or enforcement authorities.
The bill extends sexual-risk-avoidance education funding, a program oriented toward abstinence education that is generally viewed as aligned with restricting abortion access.

Title IV sets specific FY2025 funding levels for military personnel, operations and maintenance, procurement, RDT&E, and the Defense Health Program, with some rescissions but overall sustained high levels of defense spending.
EPA, Interior, and Forest Service accounts are funded at or near prior-year levels with limited adjustments; no major new regulatory expansions or rollbacks are enacted.
Funding is continued for WIC, commodity assistance, Medicaid, foster care, SSI advance payments, and related mandatory programs, preserving existing safety-net benefit levels.
Department of Education accounts receive continued funding with some reductions in specific discretionary programs; no shift toward or away from school choice is included.
The temporary scheduling order for fentanyl-related substances is extended, reinforcing stricter enforcement against these substances.
Minor technical extensions (e.g., Parole Commission) appear, but no substantive changes to sentencing, policing, or rehabilitation policy are made.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions are present.
The measure funds ongoing operations without new revenue offsets or spending cuts sufficient to reduce deficits, thereby accommodating continued deficit spending.
No provisions expand or restrict legal protections for LGBTQ+ individuals.
State and Foreign Operations accounts are continued at prior-year levels with limited adjustments; overall foreign assistance funding is maintained rather than expanded or eliminated.
A modest election-security grant program is funded; no changes to voting access or election-integrity rules are enacted.
Cybersecurity and CISA-related authorities receive routine extensions; no new regulatory framework for tech or privacy is created.
No provisions alter union rights, worker protections, or employer flexibility.
The sexual-risk-avoidance education extension has a tangential connection to programs sometimes associated with religious or moral exemptions, but the effect is minimal.
